opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting question, because I was actually quite close to that transition. Before PyTorch, a lot of us were building frameworks around the idea of a static computational graph. You declare the whole graph up front, and then the system can optimize it, schedule it, and run it efficiently. In MXNet we tried to support both: a symbolic style and an imperative style. So we already felt the tension between what's good for the system and what's good for the person writing the model.

What PyTorch got right early was recognizing that the researcher's experience matters most. If you're trying new ideas every day, you want to write normal Python, print a tensor, step through it with a debugger, and use control flow the way you naturally think about it. Eager execution made deep learning feel like ordinary programming instead of compiling a program in your head. That lowered the barrier a lot, and research moves fast, so the community followed the tool that let them iterate fastest.

At the time some of us on the systems side worried about performance. If you execute everything eagerly, you lose the global view that lets you fuse operators, plan memory, or target different hardware. But I think the lesson was that you shouldn't make the user pay for the system's convenience. Usability comes first, and then the systems people have to work harder to recover performance underneath.

That's actually what we've seen over the past several years. The ecosystem moved toward capturing graphs from eager programs, with tracing, TorchScript, and later torch.compile, plus a lot of work on ML compilers. That connects to what I care about with TVM and machine learning compilation: let people write in a flexible, Pythonic way, then have a compilation layer that brings back the optimization opportunities and maps the program onto many kinds of hardware.

So I see the early adoption of the PyTorch approach as a very healthy correction. It put developer productivity at the center, and it pushed the systems community to build better abstractions instead of asking users to bend to the system. Both sides ended up better for it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about the early adoption of the PyTorch-style approach, I think the key insight was really about putting the developer experience first. Before that, most frameworks, including some of the ones I worked on, were built around the idea of a static computation graph. You would declare the whole graph up front, compile it, and then run it. From a systems perspective that was very appealing, because once you have the full graph you can optimize memory, fuse operators, schedule things across devices, and so on.

But what the PyTorch-style, or define-by-run, approach recognized was that researchers do not think in graphs. They think in code. They want to write a loop, put a print statement in the middle, hit an error and see a normal Python stack trace. Dynamic control flow, variable-length sequences, recursive models, all of those were painful in the static world and natural in the eager world. So the early adopters were mostly researchers who valued iteration speed over peak performance, and that turned out to be exactly the right crowd to win over, because research sets the direction for the whole field.

From my side, having worked on MXNet and later on TVM, I saw this as a tradeoff that the community was willing to make very deliberately. You give up some ability to optimize globally in exchange for flexibility and debuggability. And I think that bet was correct. The interesting part is what happened afterward: once eager mode became the default way people write models, the systems problem became how to recover the optimization opportunities without taking away that experience. That is where things like tracing, graph capture, compilers like TVM and later torch.compile come in. So in a sense the PyTorch-style approach did not end the debate between flexibility and performance. It just moved the burden from the user to the compiler, which I think is where it belongs.

astra-6.text:
I think the early appeal of a PyTorch-style approach is that it fits the way researchers experiment. You write a model, run it, inspect what happens, and change it. That short feedback loop matters a lot when you don’t yet know what the right model should look like.

There’s also a familiarity to it: the framework feels like part of the programming language you’re already using. You can use ordinary control flow and debug things in a fairly direct way. That makes it easier to get started and to express new ideas.

The interesting challenge is how to preserve that experience as you pursue performance and deployment. Ideally, people can keep that flexible programming style while the underlying system does more of the work to execute it efficiently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the early adoption was really driven by the experience of researchers. When you’re exploring a new model, you want to write some code, run it immediately, inspect the values, and change things quickly. A PyTorch-style approach makes that process feel much more like ordinary Python programming.

There is a tradeoff, because a more explicit computational graph can give the system more opportunities for optimization. But I don’t think those two directions have to remain separate. You can start with an interface that is flexible and easy to use, and then bring compiler techniques underneath it to improve performance. The important thing is to let people express their ideas naturally while making the system do more of the optimization work.
